Making the Business Case for Sustainability
🌎 
Sustainability is increasingly recognized as a key driver of business efficiency and financial performance. Effective management of operational costs through energy savings, waste reduction, and optimized resource use directly impacts the bottom line, making a strong case for the adoption of green practices.
A commitment to sustainability significantly boosts brand reputation, distinguishing companies in a competitive market. As consumer preferences shift towards more ethical and environmentally friendly products, companies with strong sustainability credentials are better positioned to capture new market segments and enhance customer loyalty.
Furthermore, embracing sustainable practices opens doors to green financing opportunities, appealing to an expanding pool of investors focused on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria. This is not only advantageous for securing investment but also beneficial for long-term financial planning.
Employee attraction and retention are also influenced by a company's sustainability efforts. Businesses known for their commitment to the environment and society are more likely to attract top talent, fostering a workforce that is both skilled and highly motivated.
For companies advancing on their sustainability journey, articulating the business case to internal stakeholders is crucial for securing support and resources. Demonstrating the tangible benefits of sustainability initiatives helps align various departments towards common environmental and financial goals.
As the market continues to evolve, the integration of sustainability into business strategies is not just advisable but essential for maintaining competitiveness and ensuring long-term success.

Sustainability Maturity Levels
🌎 
Sustainability is a journey that involves progressively integrating environmental, social, and governance principles into business operations. This evolution can be mapped through five distinct levels of maturity. The journey does not include non-compliant businesses, as they operate outside the scope of sustainability and do not engage in this progressive integration.
The first level is compliance-driven, where companies meet minimum legal standards necessary for operation. The focus here is on adhering to regulations to avoid penalties, with minimal proactive engagement in sustainability.
Moving to the second level, companies become efficiency-focused. At this stage, organizations start recognizing the economic benefits of sustainability, such as cost reductions and improved operational efficiencies. This is often the first step in actively integrating sustainable practices.
The third level is strategic proactivity. Companies at this stage embed sustainability into their core business strategies. It becomes a key component of decision-making processes, guiding the company towards more sustainable practices and beyond mere compliance or efficiency.
At the fourth level, known as integrated sustainability, the principles of sustainability are deeply woven into the company’s culture. This level influences all aspects of operations and decision-making, indicating a comprehensive commitment to sustainable development.
The fifth and final level is purpose-driven, where companies have sustainability at the core of their business model. Businesses at this stage inherently address social and environmental issues through their operations and offerings, aligning their entire purpose with global sustainability goals.
This five-level framework provides a roadmap for businesses aiming to transform their impact on the world, enhancing their operations and contributing to global sustainability efforts. Each level represents a deeper commitment and a more profound integration of sustainable practices into the very fabric of the organization.

Company Websites & Filings
Public companies' investor relations webpages provide access to company reports - including its annual report, or 10-K, and quarterly filings (10-Q). While not yet required, 10-K reports often include disclosures or narrative information related to sustainability. Some companies also provide sustainability-specific reports or webpages discussing their efforts towards climate change, DEI, and other CSR-related topics.
A simple Google search for the company name + "investor relations" can help you locate these resources on a company website.
Tips for Searching the 10-K (from ACRL-BRASS)
Company statements related to social and environmental efforts often appear under "Part 1, Item 1: Business," section of the 10-K, which addresses the company's operations.
Social and governance efforts may appear under headings such as "Human Capital Management," "Culture," 'Diversity, Equity and Inclusion," or "Equity, Equality, Diversity and Inclusion."
Statements and updates related to the company's environmental consciousness may appear under headings such as "Sustainability" or "Environmental Matters."
Words and phrases for searching environmental efforts and issues within a 10-K include: "environmental," "pollution", "emissions," "energy," "sustainability," "recycling."

Jun 27, 2024 By Mary MazzoniConsumers are all ears when it comes to corporate sustainability, but many brands are staying quiet. (Image credit: CurvaBezier/Adobe Stock)
Over 80 percent of companies plan to spend more on sustainability efforts like energy efficiency, emissions reduction and pollution prevention this year. But many of them won't talk about it. 
As global regulators crack down on greenwashing and the political pushback against environmental, social and governance (ESG) principles in the U.S. continues, a growing segment of companies are staying mum about their sustainability work. 
But this play-it-safe strategy is the opposite of what stakeholders are looking for. Among U.S. consumers, 69 percent agree businesses should communicate more — not less — about what they're doing in the areas of sustainability and social impact, according to new research from TriplePundit, our parent company 3BL and the research technology firm Glow. That includes 75 percent of Gen Z and 74 percent of millennials who want to see businesses communicate more about their efforts and progress. 
What's driving the $44 billion switch to more sustainable brands?
Our latest research builds on the findings of The $44 Billion Sustainability Opportunity report we released with 3BL, Glow and panel partner Cint earlier this year. That first-of-its-kind analysis attached a dollar figure to the value of consumers switching brands for sustainability reasons — adding up to more than $44 billion across 12 industries in the U.S. alone. A quarter of the consumers we surveyed even stopped doing business with a brand in 2023 because of its social or environmental behavior.
The 2024 Consumer Insights & Sustainability Benchmark takes a closer look at what's driving this billion-dollar shift, how consumers define companies as sustainable, and what they expect from the business world this year. 
Read on for some of the standout findings, including how consumers perceive companies that stay quiet, the behaviors they're adopting for the sake of sustainability and the many reasons why the "anti-ESG" movement is failing to resonate. 
(Click to enlarge)Quiet companies leave public perception up to chance
A growing segment of consumers are willing to seek out and validate a company's sustainability information on their own. Nearly half said they search for information about businesses’ sustainability credentials using tools like Google (36 percent) or use sustainability rankings or lists available online (9 percent).
If companies choose not to communicate, consumers will make their own assumptions, and they may not always be positive. Sixty-eight percent of consumers agree with the statement: “Companies that actively communicate their sustainability efforts have a more positive impact on the environment and society, compared to those that do not.” Only 10 percent disagreed. Meanwhile, over 40 percent of consumers assume quiet companies are either “not doing anything” to reduce their environmental impact or “need more substantial environmental initiatives.”
"What we learn is that greenhushing isn’t always a huge detriment to businesses, but it misses the opportunity for business leaders to tell their own sustainability stories and be recognized by consumers," TriplePundit contributor Andrew Kaminsky wrote in the report. "Instead, with the split on how consumers perceive silent companies, business leaders essentially relinquish control and leave public perception up to chance." 
Talking about failure is good, not bad
Companies are often reluctant to talk about things that didn't go to plan. If they miss a sustainability target or sunset a social impact program after little success, it seems easier to quietly remove messaging about the effort from their websites and never mention it again. But consumers say they don't hold it against businesses when they talk about failure. Actually, it's quite the opposite.
We posed a scenario to consumers: “A company launched a program aimed at reducing its social and/or environmental impact, but it wasn’t effective. The company scrapped the program, and leadership decided to talk about the failure and what they learned with their customers and other stakeholders.”
The majority of respondents (44 percent) said they'd think better of the company "because they were transparent." Another 19 percent wouldn't feel strongly either way, saying: "Not everything is going to work, and that’s not a big deal to me." Only 14 percent would think less of the company because it hit a bump and chose to talk about it. 
"It’s all about how business leaders react to failure or underperformance," Kaminsky wrote. "If something didn’t work, discuss what you learned from it and the changes you plan to make. Looking at problems through a lens of progress and learning is better than not reporting the failure or completely ignoring it." 
(Click to enlarge.)Consumers are willing to change their behavior for sustainability, and they want companies to help 
While some in the business world question whether Americans are "ready" to change their behavior for the sake of sustainability, this narrative is increasingly at odds with how people really feel. 
Over half of Americans say they’ve already made lifestyle changes in order to reduce their impact on people and the planet. Consumers are shopping secondhand, choosing products made from recyclable materials, and seeking out consumables in reusable or refillable packaging at rates higher than we observed in 2023. Nearly half say they are flying less to reduce their carbon footprints, and around a third are eating less meat. 
Don't let the "anti-ESG" talk slow you down
"Anti-ESG" rhetoric has become more common on political campaign trails and cable news channels over recent years. Some U.S. states have even moved to restrict financial firms deemed to be associated with ESG investments from doing business within their borders. Naturally, the noise has some business leaders spooked. But when it comes to the U.S. public, anti-ESG messaging isn't exactly hitting home. 
For starters, only around a quarter of Americans even know what ESG is, with most simply using the term "sustainability" to describe efforts to safeguard communities and the environment. 
For those who do recognize the term ESG, perception is mostly positive: 69 percent of consumers said businesses should use ESG principles to quantify and improve their impact on people and the environment, compared to only 16 percent who said they shouldn't. Nearly 89 percent of consumers who recognized the term ESG said their perception of whether businesses should use ESG principles has either increased or stayed the same over the past year, with 42 percent saying: “I feel more strongly now than I did a year ago that businesses should be using ESG principles.” 
How to engage consumers
Along with insight into public preferences, the 2024 Consumer Insights & Sustainability Benchmark includes best practices for reaching and connecting with consumers based on what they told us they'd like to see. That includes how to combine data with storytelling to drive consumer trust, where to reach different audiences with sustainability messaging, and how to position corporate sustainability efforts through a solutions lens. Check out the full report for our recommendations.

Sustainability reporting / disclosure: What’s the theory? What does it actually do?
👉 Here are facts.
-------
About this post: sustainability leaders need to be catalysts. Understanding where strategy, reporting, and other aspects fit together matter a lot.
-------
1️⃣ Reporting and disclosure are widespread.
Over two-thirds (68%)of large US companies now have a dedicated ESG reporting budget.
And over 50,000 companies will be covered by CSRD – and 10,000 non-EU companies.
2️⃣ By itself, reporting / disclosure doesn’t produce financial benefit. And neither commitments nor unaudited disclosures seem to produce faster progress.
3️⃣ That doesn’t mean reporting and disclosure never matter. The idea behind them is that they:
💰 Let investors and customers to use sustainability as part of how they choose who to give their money to. This works – there’s a lot of evidence that it matters to B2B and B2C customers (Valutus has over half a million data points on four continents showing this). And there’s a lot of evidence that it matters to investors too.
 
(Sustainability is not one of the top factors for either customers or investors, but it *does* matter.)
🗣️ Enable people to pressure companies to do more. This works too – lots of companies have changed their behavior because of pressure from employees, customers, activists, and others.
🚀 Make it possible for companies to improve faster because they have consistent data. This also works – *if* the company gets its data audited. External audits make the company be more realistic about where it is and companies that get them make faster progress.
❗Summary: Reporting and disclosure aren’t free, and by themselves they don’t create value. But they can.
What you can do:
» Since reporting and disclosure are here to stay, take advantage of what’s good about it.
» Use reported data for your own decisions about suppliers.
» Audit your data (or be as rigorous as you would if it were being audited) to be more realistic about where you are and to make faster progress.

 What is Sustainability Reporting? 
Sustainability reporting is the process through which organizations measure, disclose, and communicate their environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance and impacts to stakeholders. It provides a structured way for companies to report on non-financial factors, such as carbon emissions, resource usage, labor practices, community engagement, and ethical governance.
These reports are often framed using globally accepted standards, such as the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI), Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB), Integrated Reporting (IR), or Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD).
  
 
Why Do We Need Sustainability Reporting? 
·    Stakeholder Demand: Investors, customers, employees, and regulators are increasingly seeking transparency about how companies are addressing ESG issues.
Regulatory Compliance: Many countries are mandating ESG disclosures or imposing strict reporting frameworks to promote responsible business practices.
Corporate Responsibility: Sustainability reporting is part of a company’s commitment to ethical behavior and long-term responsibility toward the environment and society.
Risk Mitigation: By identifying and addressing sustainability risks (e.g., climate change, resource scarcity), organizations can reduce vulnerabilities.
Market Differentiation: Companies with strong sustainability reports often attract more socially and environmentally conscious investors and customers.
Global Alignment: Sustainability reporting aligns with global initiatives like the UN's Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
 
Why is Sustainability Reporting Important?
v Openness: Companies show they take responsibility by sharing successes and challenges.
v Builds Trust: It helps create trust with investors and customers through a commitment to good practices.
v Boosts Brand Image: Companies that excel in sustainability often look better in Customer's Eyes.
v Focus on the Future: Reporting helps businesses think long-term about their goals.
 
How Does Sustainability Reporting Help Decision-Making? 
Better Choices: It gives leaders the insights they need to tackle environmental and social risks.
Brings Sustainability into Core Business: It helps integrate sustainability into everyday operations and planning.
Manages Risks: Companies can spot risks early, like carbon pricing, and act to avoid problems.
Engages Stakeholders: Decisions are more in sync with what investors and customers care about.
Tracks Progress: Organizations can check their sustainability goals over time and make needed changes.
Impacts Investments: Solid reports attract investors interested in sustainability. Poor reporting can scare them away.
 
Incorporating sustainability reporting helps create a culture of responsibility and better decision-making for a sustainable future.

For companies advancing on their sustainability journey, articulating the business case to internal stakeholders is crucial for securing support and resources. Demonstrating the tangible benefits of sustainability initiatives helps align various departments towards common environmental and financial goals.
As the market continues to evolve, the integration of sustainability into business strategies is not just advisable but essential for maintaining competitiveness and ensuring long-term success.

Sustainability Maturity Levels
🌎 
Sustainability is a journey that involves progressively integrating environmental, social, and governance principles into business operations. This evolution can be mapped through five distinct levels of maturity. The journey does not include non-compliant businesses, as they operate outside the scope of sustainability and do not engage in this progressive integration.
The first level is compliance-driven, where companies meet minimum legal standards necessary for operation. The focus here is on adhering to regulations to avoid penalties, with minimal proactive engagement in sustainability.
Moving to the second level, companies become efficiency-focused. At this stage, organizations start recognizing the economic benefits of sustainability, such as cost reductions and improved operational efficiencies. This is often the first step in actively integrating sustainable practices.
The third level is strategic proactivity. Companies at this stage embed sustainability into their core business strategies. It becomes a key component of decision-making processes, guiding the company towards more sustainable practices and beyond mere compliance or efficiency.
At the fourth level, known as integrated sustainability, the principles of sustainability are deeply woven into the company’s culture. This level influences all aspects of operations and decision-making, indicating a comprehensive commitment to sustainable development.
The fifth and final level is purpose-driven, where companies have sustainability at the core of their business model. Businesses at this stage inherently address social and environmental issues through their operations and offerings, aligning their entire purpose with global sustainability goals.
This five-level framework provides a roadmap for businesses aiming to transform their impact on the world, enhancing their operations and contributing to global sustainability efforts. Each level represents a deeper commitment and a more profound integration of sustainable practices into the very fabric of the organization.

Integrating sustainability into the organization
🌎 
Aligning sustainability with business strategy is essential for any organization committed to making a substantial impact. This alignment ensures that sustainability principles are not just peripheral considerations but are integral to the overarching business objectives.
Incorporation of sustainability into core workflows and processes is another critical step. It allows organizations to seamlessly integrate these principles into the day-to-day operations, making sustainability a natural part of business practice rather than an imposed addition.
Defining clear roles and responsibilities within the organization is also crucial. This clarity enables effective action and accountability, ensuring that every team member understands their role in contributing to sustainability goals.
Including sustainability considerations, data, and metrics in key business decisions is imperative. This approach ensures that decisions are made not only with financial outcomes in mind but also with consideration for environmental and social impacts.
By embedding sustainability at these various levels, organizations can achieve a more profound and lasting impact. This comprehensive approach transforms how businesses operate, leading to innovations and efficiencies that benefit both the company and the planet.
Organizations are encouraged to adopt these practices to not just meet the minimum standards but to lead in sustainability, setting a benchmark in their industries.
Source: IBM

Ultimately, the integration of sustainability at these levels does more than just protect the planet; it positions organizations as leaders in their industries, setting new benchmarks and driving progress. Companies that embrace this comprehensive approach will not only meet the rising expectations of consumers and stakeholders but will also unlock new avenues for innovation and value creation.
In a world where sustainability is no longer optional, businesses that lead with purpose will be the ones that not only survive but thrive. Let’s set the standard, inspire change, and drive a future where business success and sustainability go hand in hand.

- Measurable outcomes
- Resource planning
- Assigned responsibilities
- Timelines and milestones
- Risk assessment

Three ways to approach sustainability
🌎 
In the journey towards sustainability, businesses often adopt one of three distinct approaches, yet only one consistently delivers substantial value. 
Initially, some opt for a compliance-focused method, prioritizing adherence to external regulations and managing reputational risks. This approach, while addressing immediate concerns, is limited by internal constraints that prevent meaningful action. It tends to keep sustainability at arm's length, treating it more as a necessity for risk mitigation than a strategic opportunity.
Another strategy involves treating sustainability as a standalone project. This method establishes a dedicated department tasked with spearheading sustainability initiatives, which liaises directly with top management. 
Despite its intentions, this approach only partially integrates sustainability into the broader business operations, maintaining it as a somewhat separate entity. It steps forward from mere compliance, attempting to weave sustainability into the organizational fabric, yet stops short of full integration.
The third and most effective approach embeds sustainability into the very core of business strategy. Unlike the previous methods, this approach ensures sustainability considerations are ingrained in every decision-making process across all levels of the organization. 
It transforms sustainability from an isolated effort into a central pillar of the company's governance and operational framework, thus achieving a comprehensive and enduring impact.
This embedded approach unlocks a multitude of benefits, far beyond compliance or reputational management. By making sustainability a foundational element, businesses can innovate more freely, adapt to changes more resiliently, and tap into new markets with greater ease. 
It marks a shift from viewing sustainability as an external requirement or isolated initiative to recognizing it as an intrinsic part of strategic planning and execution.
Moreover, embedding sustainability paves the way for a holistic transformation within organizations. It necessitates a reevaluation of practices, encouraging a shift towards more sustainable operations and decision-making processes that consider long-term impacts. This not only enhances the organization's contribution to global sustainability goals but also aligns it with the growing societal and consumer expectations for responsible business conduct.

Jun 27, 2024 By Mary MazzoniConsumers are all ears when it comes to corporate sustainability, but many brands are staying quiet. (Image credit: CurvaBezier/Adobe Stock)
Over 80 percent of companies plan to spend more on sustainability efforts like energy efficiency, emissions reduction and pollution prevention this year. But many of them won't talk about it. 
As global regulators crack down on greenwashing and the political pushback against environmental, social and governance (ESG) principles in the U.S. continues, a growing segment of companies are staying mum about their sustainability work. 
But this play-it-safe strategy is the opposite of what stakeholders are looking for. Among U.S. consumers, 69 percent agree businesses should communicate more — not less — about what they're doing in the areas of sustainability and social impact, according to new research from TriplePundit, our parent company 3BL and the research technology firm Glow. That includes 75 percent of Gen Z and 74 percent of millennials who want to see businesses communicate more about their efforts and progress. 
What's driving the $44 billion switch to more sustainable brands?
Our latest research builds on the findings of The $44 Billion Sustainability Opportunity report we released with 3BL, Glow and panel partner Cint earlier this year. That first-of-its-kind analysis attached a dollar figure to the value of consumers switching brands for sustainability reasons — adding up to more than $44 billion across 12 industries in the U.S. alone. A quarter of the consumers we surveyed even stopped doing business with a brand in 2023 because of its social or environmental behavior.
The 2024 Consumer Insights & Sustainability Benchmark takes a closer look at what's driving this billion-dollar shift, how consumers define companies as sustainable, and what they expect from the business world this year. 
Read on for some of the standout findings, including how consumers perceive companies that stay quiet, the behaviors they're adopting for the sake of sustainability and the many reasons why the "anti-ESG" movement is failing to resonate. 
(Click to enlarge)Quiet companies leave public perception up to chance
A growing segment of consumers are willing to seek out and validate a company's sustainability information on their own. Nearly half said they search for information about businesses’ sustainability credentials using tools like Google (36 percent) or use sustainability rankings or lists available online (9 percent).
If companies choose not to communicate, consumers will make their own assumptions, and they may not always be positive. Sixty-eight percent of consumers agree with the statement: “Companies that actively communicate their sustainability efforts have a more positive impact on the environment and society, compared to those that do not.” Only 10 percent disagreed. Meanwhile, over 40 percent of consumers assume quiet companies are either “not doing anything” to reduce their environmental impact or “need more substantial environmental initiatives.”
"What we learn is that greenhushing isn’t always a huge detriment to businesses, but it misses the opportunity for business leaders to tell their own sustainability stories and be recognized by consumers," TriplePundit contributor Andrew Kaminsky wrote in the report. "Instead, with the split on how consumers perceive silent companies, business leaders essentially relinquish control and leave public perception up to chance." 
Talking about failure is good, not bad
Companies are often reluctant to talk about things that didn't go to plan. If they miss a sustainability target or sunset a social impact program after little success, it seems easier to quietly remove messaging about the effort from their websites and never mention it again. But consumers say they don't hold it against businesses when they talk about failure. Actually, it's quite the opposite.
We posed a scenario to consumers: “A company launched a program aimed at reducing its social and/or environmental impact, but it wasn’t effective. The company scrapped the program, and leadership decided to talk about the failure and what they learned with their customers and other stakeholders.”
The majority of respondents (44 percent) said they'd think better of the company "because they were transparent." Another 19 percent wouldn't feel strongly either way, saying: "Not everything is going to work, and that’s not a big deal to me." Only 14 percent would think less of the company because it hit a bump and chose to talk about it. 
"It’s all about how business leaders react to failure or underperformance," Kaminsky wrote. "If something didn’t work, discuss what you learned from it and the changes you plan to make. Looking at problems through a lens of progress and learning is better than not reporting the failure or completely ignoring it." 
(Click to enlarge.)Consumers are willing to change their behavior for sustainability, and they want companies to help 
While some in the business world question whether Americans are "ready" to change their behavior for the sake of sustainability, this narrative is increasingly at odds with how people really feel. 
Over half of Americans say they’ve already made lifestyle changes in order to reduce their impact on people and the planet. Consumers are shopping secondhand, choosing products made from recyclable materials, and seeking out consumables in reusable or refillable packaging at rates higher than we observed in 2023. Nearly half say they are flying less to reduce their carbon footprints, and around a third are eating less meat. 
Don't let the "anti-ESG" talk slow you down
"Anti-ESG" rhetoric has become more common on political campaign trails and cable news channels over recent years. Some U.S. states have even moved to restrict financial firms deemed to be associated with ESG investments from doing business within their borders. Naturally, the noise has some business leaders spooked. But when it comes to the U.S. public, anti-ESG messaging isn't exactly hitting home. 
For starters, only around a quarter of Americans even know what ESG is, with most simply using the term "sustainability" to describe efforts to safeguard communities and the environment. 
For those who do recognize the term ESG, perception is mostly positive: 69 percent of consumers said businesses should use ESG principles to quantify and improve their impact on people and the environment, compared to only 16 percent who said they shouldn't. Nearly 89 percent of consumers who recognized the term ESG said their perception of whether businesses should use ESG principles has either increased or stayed the same over the past year, with 42 percent saying: “I feel more strongly now than I did a year ago that businesses should be using ESG principles.” 
How to engage consumers
Along with insight into public preferences, the 2024 Consumer Insights & Sustainability Benchmark includes best practices for reaching and connecting with consumers based on what they told us they'd like to see. That includes how to combine data with storytelling to drive consumer trust, where to reach different audiences with sustainability messaging, and how to position corporate sustainability efforts through a solutions lens. For the first time, TIME and data firm Statista have created a rigorous methodology with which to measure the world’s most sustainable companies for 2024. The companies at the top of the list have signed on to some of the most respected climate programs, including the 1.5°C target from the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), and receive high scores from CDP (formerly the Carbon Disclosure Project). TIME and Statista further held companies to high standards for their Scope 1 and 2 emissions and energy consumption relative to company size, emissions reductions in 2021 and 2022 (the most recent years fully reported), and proportion of renewable energy used by the company’s operations. (Scope 1 emissions are directly caused by a company; Scope 2 are indirectly created when a company purchases power.) And, perhaps most importantly, many of the top companies have incorporated sustainability into their business models. Schneider Electric, for instance, which is based in France and tops the list, creates software and services for energy management. It has not only set ambitious targets to reduce its own emissions—carbon neutral by 2025—but also helps its customers reduce emissions and become more energy efficient through its Sustainability Business. It has its own sustainability impact program to track its performance, and has also reduced emissions across its supply chain. Schneider has received a climate score of “A” from the CDP for 12 years in a row. “We’ve positioned the company to be an impact company,” CEO Peter W. Herweck said on a recent earnings call.While many companies that ranked highly are in industries that don’t make many physical products—like banking, tech, and consulting—there were companies that showed sustainability is possible even if you make things. Illumina, the U.S. biotechnology company that's fifth on the list, recently debuted its most powerful gene sequencer while also reducing packaging waste by 90% from the previous model. Moncler, the Italian luxury fashion house, ranked third on the list by using recycled materials, recycling more than 80% of its nylon scraps in 2023, and using 100% renewable energy at its directly managed offices, stores, factories, and logistics hubs. “While we take pride in this achievement, we are aware much remains to be done,” said Remo Ruffini, chairman and CEO of Moncler S.p.A, when the company was named to the Dow Jones Sustainability Indices in 2023. While impressive, Schneider’s top score of 88.86 out of 100 on TIME’s list shows the distance even the most dedicated companies have to go to be truly sustainable.
